topics.title: Algebra skills for Methods
points: Expand with the distributive law; factorise by taking out common factors, then by recognising patterns.
Perfect squares: \((a \pm b)^2 = a^2 \pm 2ab + b^2\). Difference of two squares: \(a^2 - b^2 = (a - b)(a + b)\).
Surds: \(\sqrt{ab} = \sqrt{a}\sqrt{b}\); rationalise a denominator by multiplying by a suitable form of 1.
Rearrange formulas by doing the same thing to both sides; when an inequality is multiplied or divided by a negative number, reverse the sign.
topics.explain: Explain why \(\sqrt{9 + 16}\) is not equal to \(\sqrt{9} + \sqrt{16}\), and what rule people are wrongly applying when they think it is.

p: This is the first lesson in Methods. It reviews the algebra from Years 9 and 10 that every later lesson assumes.

The big idea: Methods is mostly about functions and calculus, but most lost marks come from algebra slips. Fluent, accurate algebra frees your attention for the new ideas. Work through every example by hand, without a calculator.
Multiply every term in one bracket by every term in the other: \((2x - 3)(x + 4) = 2x^2 + 8x - 3x - 12 = 2x^2 + 5x - 12\).
Patterns save time: \((x + 5)^2 = x^2 + 10x + 25\); \((3x - 2)^2 = 9x^2 - 12x + 4\); \((x - 7)(x + 7) = x^2 - 49\). For three brackets, expand two first, then multiply by the third.
Always take out the highest common factor first: \(6x^2 - 9x = 3x(2x - 3)\).

Then look for a pattern. Difference of two squares: \(4x^2 - 25 = (2x - 5)(2x + 5)\). Perfect square: \(x^2 - 8x + 16 = (x - 4)^2\). Monic quadratic \(x^2 + bx + c\): find two numbers that multiply to \(c\) and add to \(b\): \(x^2 - x - 12 = (x - 4)(x + 3)\).

Non-monic quadratic, \(6x^2 + x - 2\): find two numbers that multiply to \(6 \times (-2) = -12\) and add to 1: 4 and \(-3\). Split the middle term: \(6x^2 + 4x - 3x - 2 = 2x(3x + 2) - (3x + 2) = (2x - 1)(3x + 2)\).
check: Numbers multiplying to \(-24\) and adding to 10 are 12 and \(-2\): \(3x^2 + 12x - 2x - 8 = 3x(x + 4) - 2(x + 4) = (3x - 2)(x + 4)\).

p: Simplify \(\dfrac{12a^5b^2}{4a^2b^3} = 3a^3b^{-1} = \dfrac{3a^3}{b}\). A fractional index is a root: \(x^{\frac{1}{2}} = \sqrt{x}\), \(x^{\frac{3}{2}} = \left(\sqrt{x}\right)^3\).

Simplify surds by taking out square factors: \(\sqrt{72} = \sqrt{36 \times 2} = 6\sqrt{2}\). Only like surds can be added: \(3\sqrt{2} + 5\sqrt{2} = 8\sqrt{2}\), but \(\sqrt{2} + \sqrt{3}\) cannot be simplified.

Rationalise: \(\dfrac{6}{\sqrt{3}} = \dfrac{6\sqrt{3}}{3} = 2\sqrt{3}\). For a binomial denominator use the conjugate: \(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5} - 1} \times \dfrac{\sqrt{5} + 1}{\sqrt{5} + 1} = \dfrac{\sqrt{5} + 1}{4}\).
Solve \(\dfrac{2x - 1}{3} = \dfrac{x + 4}{2}\): multiply both sides by 6: \(2(2x - 1) = 3(x + 4)\), so \(4x - 2 = 3x + 12\) and \(x = 14\).
Inequalities work the same way, except that multiplying or dividing by a negative number reverses the sign: \(5 - 2x > 11 \Rightarrow -2x > 6 \Rightarrow x < -3\).

Rearranging a formula (a literal equation) uses the same steps with letters. Make \(r\) the subject of \(A = \pi r^2\): \(r = \sqrt{\dfrac{A}{\pi}}\) (taking the positive root because \(r\) is a length). Make \(x\) the subject of \(y = \dfrac{x + 2}{x - 1}\): \(y(x - 1) = x + 2 \Rightarrow xy - x = y + 2 \Rightarrow x(y - 1) = y + 2 \Rightarrow x = \dfrac{y + 2}{y - 1}\).
Elimination: \(3x + 2y = 16\) and \(x - 2y = 0\). Adding removes \(y\): \(4x = 16\), so \(x = 4\) and \(y = 2\).
Substitution suits an equation already solved for one variable: \(y = 2x - 1\) and \(3x + y = 9\) gives \(3x + 2x - 1 = 9\), so \(x = 2\), \(y = 3\). Check the solution in both original equations.

\((a + b)^2 = a^2 + b^2\): the middle term \(2ab\) is missing. \(\sqrt{a + b} = \sqrt{a} + \sqrt{b}\): false. Cancelling terms instead of factors: \(\dfrac{x + 6}{x}\) is not 7. Forgetting to reverse an inequality. Dropping a negative sign when expanding \(-(x - 3)\).

qs.e: Perfect square: the middle term is twice the product.

qs.q: Make \(t\) the subject of \(v = u + at\).

qs.e: Dividing by a negative reverses the inequality.

s: Subtract, taking care with the sign: \(4x^2 + 4x + 1 - x^2 + 9 = 3x^2 + 4x + 10\).

qs.q: Solve the simultaneous equations \(2x + y = 7\) and \(x - y = 2\).

s: Collect the \(x\) terms on one side: \(xy - 3x = -1 - 2y\).

topics.title: Relations, functions and notation
points: A relation is a set of ordered pairs; a function is a relation in which each input gives exactly one output.
Vertical line test: a graph is a function if no vertical line meets it more than once.
Function notation: \(f(x)\) is the output when the input is \(x\); \(f: D \to \mathbb{R}\) states the domain \(D\).
The domain is the set of allowed inputs; the range is the set of outputs. Use interval notation: \([a, b]\), \((a, b)\), \([a, \infty)\).
The implied (maximal) domain excludes inputs that cause division by zero or the square root of a negative number.
topics.explain: Explain to a friend why a circle is not the graph of a function, but the top half of a circle is.

p: Before this lesson you should be confident with the algebra skills lesson.

The big idea: a function is a rule that turns each input into exactly one output. Almost everything in Methods is a function, so the language of this lesson (domain, range, notation) is used in every later lesson. Getting it precise now prevents a lot of lost marks.

A relation is any set of ordered pairs, such as \(\{(1, 2), (2, 4), (3, 6)\}\) or all the points on a circle. A function is a special relation: no input is paired with two different outputs. \(\{(1, 2), (1, 3)\}\) is not a function because 1 has two outputs.

Relations are classified by how inputs and outputs pair up: one-to-one (\(y = 2x\)), many-to-one (\(y = x^2\), since 2 and \(-2\) both give 4), one-to-many (\(x = y^2\)) and many-to-many (a circle). Only one-to-one and many-to-one relations are functions.
The vertical line test checks a graph: if any vertical line cuts it more than once, some input has two outputs, so it is not a function.
check: No. For \(x = 4\), \(y = 2\) or \(y = -2\), so one input has two outputs (it fails the vertical line test).

p: If \(f(x) = x^2 - 3x\), then \(f(5) = 25 - 15 = 10\), \(f(-1) = 1 + 3 = 4\) and \(f(a + 1) = (a + 1)^2 - 3(a + 1) = a^2 - a - 2\). Replace every \(x\) with the input, using brackets.
Solving \(f(x) = 4\) means finding the inputs that give an output of 4: \(x^2 - 3x - 4 = 0\), so \(x = 4\) or \(x = -1\).
The full description of a function names its domain: \(f: [0, 5] \to \mathbb{R},\ f(x) = x^2 - 3x\). The arrow notation says “\(f\) maps numbers in \([0, 5]\) to real numbers”.

Interval notation: square brackets include an endpoint, round brackets exclude it. \([2, 5)\) means \(2 \le x < 5\). \((-\infty, 3]\) means \(x \le 3\). \(\mathbb{R}\) is all real numbers; \(\mathbb{R} \setminus \{1\}\) is all real numbers except 1.

To find the range, sketch the graph over the domain and read the lowest and highest \(y\)-values, watching for turning points inside the domain. Example: \(f: [-1, 4] \to \mathbb{R},\ f(x) = (x - 1)^2\). The minimum is 0 at \(x = 1\); the endpoints give \(f(-1) = 4\) and \(f(4) = 9\). Range: \([0, 9]\). The range is not simply \([f(-1), f(4)]\).
check: The function is increasing: \(f(-2) = -3\) (excluded) and \(f(3) = 7\) (included), so the range is \((-3, 7]\).

p: When no domain is stated, use the largest set of real numbers for which the rule works. Two restrictions matter in Units 1 and 2: no division by zero, and no square root of a negative number.

\(f(x) = \dfrac{1}{x - 2}\): domain \(\mathbb{R} \setminus \{2\}\). \(g(x) = \sqrt{3 - x}\): need \(3 - x \ge 0\), so domain \((-\infty, 3]\). \(h(x) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x + 1}}\): need \(x + 1 > 0\), so domain \((-1, \infty)\). Logarithms add a third restriction later: the input must be positive.
A hybrid (piecewise) function uses different rules on different parts of its domain: \(f(x) = \begin{cases} x + 2, & x < 0 \\ x^2, & x \ge 0 \end{cases}\).

To evaluate, first choose the right piece: \(f(-3) = -1\), \(f(3) = 9\), and \(f(0) = 0\) because 0 belongs to the second piece. Sketch each piece only over its own interval, with a closed circle for an included endpoint and an open circle for an excluded one. This function has a break at \(x = 0\): the first piece approaches 2 but the second starts at 0.

The inverse of a relation swaps every input and output, which reflects its graph in the line \(y = x\). The inverse of \(y = 2x + 1\) is \(x = 2y + 1\), or \(y = \dfrac{x - 1}{2}\). The inverse is itself a function only if the original was one-to-one. Units 3 and 4 develop this in detail.

Finding the range from the endpoints alone when there is a turning point in between. Using a round bracket for an included endpoint. Writing \(f(a + 1) = f(a) + 1\). Forgetting the brackets when substituting a negative number: \(f(-1)\) for \(x^2\) is \((-1)^2 = 1\), not \(-1\).

qs.e: Each input of a cubic has one output.

qs.q: State the range of \(f: [-3, 2] \to \mathbb{R},\ f(x) = x^2\).
What does the vertical line test check, and why does it work?
qs.a: Whether a graph represents a function. If a vertical line meets the graph more than once, one input has more than one output.

qs.e: Square bracket includes, round bracket excludes.
Division by zero happens only at x = −3.

qs.q: The range of \(f: [-1, 2] \to \mathbb{R},\ f(x) = x^2 - 2x\) is…
qs.e: Turning point \((1, -1)\) is inside the domain; \(f(-1) = 3\) and \(f(2) = 0\).

qs.q: \(f(x) = \begin{cases} 1 - x, & x < 1 \\ x^2, & x \ge 1 \end{cases}\). Find \(f(0) + f(3)\).
s: 0 is less than 1, so use the first rule: \(f(0) = 1 - 0 = 1\).
3 is at least 1, so use the second rule: \(f(3) = 9\).

topics.title: Linear and quadratic functions
points: Gradient: \(m = \dfrac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1}\). Equation of a line: \(y - y_1 = m(x - x_1)\).
Parallel lines have equal gradients. Perpendicular lines: \(m_1 \times m_2 = -1\).
Midpoint: \(\left(\dfrac{x_1 + x_2}{2}, \dfrac{y_1 + y_2}{2}\right)\). Distance: \(\sqrt{(x_2 - x_1)^2 + (y_2 - y_1)^2}\).
Quadratic formula: \(x = \dfrac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}\) for \(ax^2 + bx + c = 0\).
Turning point form \(y = a(x - h)^2 + k\) has turning point \((h, k)\).
Discriminant \(\Delta = b^2 - 4ac\): \(\Delta > 0\) two real solutions, \(\Delta = 0\) one, \(\Delta < 0\) none.
topics.explain: Explain what the discriminant tells you about where a parabola meets the \(x\)-axis.

qs.q: Find the gradient of the line through \((1, 2)\) and \((4, 11)\).
How many real solutions does \(2x^2 + 3x + 5 = 0\) have?
A line is perpendicular to one with gradient \(2\). Its gradient is…
Find the turning point of \(y = x^2 - 8x + 3\).
s: Turning point form \(y = (x - h)^2 + k\) gives \((h, k) = (4, -13)\), a minimum.

qs.q: For which values of \(k\) does \(x^2 + kx + 9 = 0\) have two distinct real solutions?
The line through \((1, 2)\) parallel to \(y = 3x + 5\) is…
Find the midpoint of, and the distance between, \((-1, 3)\) and \((5, -5)\).

p: Before this lesson you should be confident with the algebra skills lesson: expanding, factorising and rearranging.

The big idea: linear and quadratic functions are the simplest curves in Methods, and almost every technique you will use later (finding intercepts, solving equations, finding where graphs meet, modelling a situation) appears here first in its simplest form. Master them and the harder functions feel familiar.

A straight line is fixed by its gradient and one point. Gradient–intercept form \(y = mx + c\) shows the gradient and \(y\)-intercept. Point–gradient form \(y - y_1 = m(x - x_1)\) is quickest when you know a point. The gradient is also \(\tan\theta\), where \(\theta\) is the angle the line makes with the positive \(x\)-axis.
Distance between two points: \(d = \sqrt{(x_2 - x_1)^2 + (y_2 - y_1)^2}\). Two lines are parallel when their gradients are equal, and perpendicular when the gradients multiply to \(-1\).
Find the line through \((2, 5)\) perpendicular to \(y = 2x - 1\).
The given gradient is 2, so the perpendicular gradient is \(-\tfrac{1}{2}\). \(y - 5 = -\tfrac{1}{2}(x - 2)\), which gives \(y = -\tfrac{1}{2}x + 6\).

General form \(y = ax^2 + bx + c\) shows the \(y\)-intercept \(c\). Factorised form \(y = a(x - p)(x - q)\) shows the \(x\)-intercepts \(p\) and \(q\). Turning point form \(y = a(x - h)^2 + k\) shows the turning point \((h, k)\). The axis of symmetry is \(x = -\dfrac{b}{2a}\). If \(a > 0\) the parabola has a minimum; if \(a < 0\), a maximum.
Write \(y = 2x^2 - 12x + 10\) in turning point form.
\(y = 2(x^2 - 6x) + 10 = 2\big((x - 3)^2 - 9\big) + 10 = 2(x - 3)^2 - 8\). Turning point \((3, -8)\), a minimum. Intercepts: \(2(x - 3)^2 = 8 \Rightarrow x = 1\) or \(x = 5\).

The discriminant tells you how many times a parabola meets the \(x\)-axis, and more generally how many solutions any quadratic equation has. It is the tool for “find the values of \(k\) for which…” questions.

Example: for what values of \(k\) does \(x^2 + kx + 9 = 0\) have no real solutions? \(\Delta = k^2 - 36 < 0\), so \(-6 < k < 6\). To find where a line is tangent to a parabola, set the two equal and require \(\Delta = 0\).
check: \(\Delta = 16 - 16 = 0\), so one: the graph touches the axis at \(x = 2\).

p: Factorising is quickest when it works: \(x^2 - 5x + 6 = 0 \Rightarrow (x - 2)(x - 3) = 0 \Rightarrow x = 2\) or \(x = 3\). It relies on the null factor law: if a product is zero, one of the factors is zero.
Completing the square works for any quadratic and shows the turning point: \(x^2 + 6x + 2 = 0 \Rightarrow (x + 3)^2 - 7 = 0 \Rightarrow x = -3 \pm \sqrt{7}\).

The quadratic formula always works: for \(2x^2 + 3x - 4 = 0\), \(x = \dfrac{-3 \pm \sqrt{9 + 32}}{4} = \dfrac{-3 \pm \sqrt{41}}{4}\). Try factorising first; if the discriminant is not a perfect square, the quadratic will not factorise over the rationals, so use the formula.

To find intersection points, set the rules equal and solve. Example: \(y = x + 1\) and \(y = x^2 - 1\). \(x^2 - 1 = x + 1 \Rightarrow x^2 - x - 2 = 0 \Rightarrow (x - 2)(x + 1) = 0\). The points are \((2, 3)\) and \((-1, 0)\): substitute each \(x\) back into either rule to get \(y\).

The discriminant of the combined equation tells you how many times they meet. Example: for what value of \(k\) is \(y = 2x + k\) a tangent to \(y = x^2\)? \(x^2 - 2x - k = 0\) must have exactly one solution, so \(\Delta = 4 + 4k = 0\) and \(k = -1\). The point of contact is \((1, 1)\).
A ball is thrown so that its height is \(h = -5t^2 + 20t + 1.5\) metres after \(t\) seconds. Completing the square: \(h = -5(t - 2)^2 + 21.5\), so the maximum height is 21.5 m at \(t = 2\) s.

It lands when \(h = 0\): \(t = \dfrac{-20 \pm \sqrt{400 + 30}}{-10}\). The positive solution is \(t = \dfrac{20 + \sqrt{430}}{10} \approx 4.07\) s. The model only makes sense for \(0 \le t \le 4.07\); outside that domain the rule gives meaningless heights. Always state a sensible domain for a model.

Forgetting to factor out \(a\) before completing the square. Losing the \(\pm\) when taking a square root. Dividing an equation by \(x\) and losing the solution \(x = 0\). Writing a perpendicular gradient as the reciprocal without changing the sign.

topics.title: Polynomials and transformations
points: Remainder theorem: dividing \(P(x)\) by \((x - a)\) leaves remainder \(P(a)\).
Factor theorem: if \(P(a) = 0\), then \((x - a)\) is a factor of \(P(x)\).
Cubics: find one factor by trial (try factors of the constant term), then divide to get a quadratic.
A repeated factor \((x - a)^2\) touches the \(x\)-axis; \((x - a)^3\) gives a stationary point of inflection.

Transformations of \(y = f(x)\): \(y = a f(x)\) dilates by factor \(a\) from the \(x\)-axis; \(y = f(bx)\) dilates by factor \(\tfrac{1}{b}\) from the \(y\)-axis; \(y = -f(x)\) reflects in the \(x\)-axis; \(y = f(x - h) + k\) translates \(h\) right and \(k\) up.
Power functions: \(y = x^n\); \(y = \dfrac{1}{x}\) (asymptotes \(x = 0\), \(y = 0\)); \(y = \sqrt{x}\).
topics.explain: Explain how the graph of \(y = (x - 2)^2 + 3\) is obtained from \(y = x^2\).

qs.q: Find the remainder when \(x^3 + 2x - 1\) is divided by \((x - 2)\).

s: Try factors of 6: \(P(1) = 1 - 2 - 5 + 6 = 0\), so \(x - 1\) is a factor.

qs.q: The remainder when \(2x^3 + x - 4\) is divided by \(x + 1\) is…
\(x - 2\) is a factor of \(x^3 + ax^2 - 4\). Find \(a\).

qs.e: A squared factor gives a touching point.

qs.q: Describe the transformations that take \(y = x^3\) to \(y = 2(x - 1)^3 + 4\).
qs.a: Dilation by factor 2 from the x-axis, then translation 1 unit right and 4 units up.

s: Bring everything to one side: \(x^3 - 4x = 0\). Do not divide by \(x\), which would lose \(x = 0\).

p: Before this lesson you should be confident with quadratics, including factorising and sketching.

The big idea: higher-degree polynomials behave like quadratics with more turns. Once you can find one factor, the rest reduces to a quadratic you already know how to handle, and the factors tell you almost everything about the graph.

The degree of a polynomial is its highest power. A polynomial of degree \(n\) has at most \(n\) real roots and at most \(n - 1\) turning points. To divide by a linear factor, use long division or equate coefficients: \(P(x) = (x - a)Q(x) + R\).
Factorise \(P(x) = x^3 - 4x^2 + x + 6\) and solve \(P(x) = 0\).

Mark the \(x\)-intercepts from the factors and the \(y\)-intercept from \(P(0)\). Use the sign of the leading coefficient for the end behaviour: a positive cubic goes from bottom left to top right; a positive quartic goes up at both ends. At a single factor the graph crosses the axis. At a squared factor it touches and turns. At a cubed factor it flattens as it crosses (a stationary point of inflection).

Three kinds change a graph. A dilation stretches or compresses it from an axis. A reflection flips it in an axis. A translation shifts it. For \(y = a f\big(n(x - h)\big) + k\): dilation by factor \(a\) from the \(x\)-axis, dilation by factor \(\tfrac{1}{n}\) from the \(y\)-axis, then translation \(h\) units in the positive \(x\) direction and \(k\) units in the positive \(y\) direction. A negative \(a\) reflects in the \(x\)-axis; a negative \(n\) reflects in the \(y\)-axis.
Changes inside the bracket act on \(x\) and work in the opposite way to how they look: \(f(x - 3)\) moves the graph right, and \(f(2x)\) halves the horizontal distances.
Describe how \(y = x^2\) becomes \(y = -2(x + 1)^2 + 3\).

Dilation by factor 2 from the \(x\)-axis, reflection in the \(x\)-axis, translation 1 unit in the negative \(x\) direction and 3 units in the positive \(y\) direction. The turning point moves from \((0, 0)\) to \((-1, 3)\).

\(y = \dfrac{a}{x - h} + k\) is a hyperbola with asymptotes \(x = h\) and \(y = k\). \(y = \dfrac{a}{(x - h)^2} + k\) is a truncus with the same asymptotes but both branches on the same side. \(y = a\sqrt{x - h} + k\) starts at \((h, k)\) and has domain \(x \ge h\). Always label asymptotes with their equations and give intercepts as coordinates.

Divide \(x^3 + 2x^2 - 5x - 6\) by \(x + 1\). \(x^3 \div x = x^2\); multiply back \(x^2(x + 1) = x^3 + x^2\) and subtract to get \(x^2 - 5x\). \(x^2 \div x = x\); subtract \(x(x + 1)\) to get \(-6x - 6\). \(-6x \div x = -6\); subtract \(-6(x + 1)\) to get 0.

So \(x^3 + 2x^2 - 5x - 6 = (x + 1)(x^2 + x - 6) = (x + 1)(x + 3)(x - 2)\). Check by expanding. A zero remainder confirms that \(x + 1\) is a factor, which the factor theorem predicts because \(P(-1) = -1 + 2 + 5 - 6 = 0\).
check: Find the remainder when \(P(x) = x^3 - 3x + 5\) is divided by \(x - 2\).

notes.h: Finding a rule from a graph
p: A cubic has \(x\)-intercepts at \(-2\), 1 and 3 and a \(y\)-intercept of 12. Its rule is \(y = a(x + 2)(x - 1)(x - 3)\). Substitute \(x = 0\): \(a(2)(-1)(-3) = 6a = 12\), so \(a = 2\).

If the graph touches the axis at \(x = 1\) and crosses at \(x = -3\), the factors are \((x - 1)^2(x + 3)\). If it flattens as it crosses at \(x = 2\), the factor is \((x - 2)^3\). Read the behaviour at each intercept, write the factors, then use one other point to find \(a\).
check: A cubic has \(x\)-intercepts 0, 2 and 5 and passes through \((1, 8)\). Find its rule.

notes.h: Sum and difference of two cubes
p: Example: \(x^3 - 8 = (x - 2)(x^2 + 2x + 4)\). The quadratic factor has \(\Delta = 4 - 16 < 0\), so it has no real roots and \(x^3 - 8 = 0\) has only the solution \(x = 2\).
Writing a translation of \(f(x + 2)\) as 2 to the right. Listing transformations in an order that does not produce the rule. Drawing a graph that touches or crosses an asymptote it should approach.

topics.title: Exponential and logarithmic functions
points: Index laws: \(a^m \times a^n = a^{m+n}\), \(\dfrac{a^m}{a^n} = a^{m-n}\), \((a^m)^n = a^{mn}\), \(a^0 = 1\), \(a^{-n} = \dfrac{1}{a^n}\).
Definition: \(\log_a x = y \iff a^y = x\). Natural log: \(\log_e x\) (also written \(\ln x\)).
Log laws: \(\log_a(xy) = \log_a x + \log_a y\), \(\log_a\left(\dfrac{x}{y}\right) = \log_a x - \log_a y\), \(\log_a(x^n) = n\log_a x\).
\(y = a^x\) has asymptote \(y = 0\) and passes through \((0, 1)\). \(y = \log_a x\) has asymptote \(x = 0\) and passes through \((1, 0)\).
Solve exponential equations by matching bases or taking logs of both sides.

qs.q: Solve \(3^x = 10\), exactly and to three decimal places.
A population is \(P = 500e^{0.1t}\) after \(t\) years. When does it reach 1000?

p: Before this lesson you should be confident with index laws and with transformations of graphs.

The big idea: exponential functions model anything that grows or shrinks by the same factor in equal time steps, such as populations, investments and radioactive decay. Logarithms are the tool for undoing an exponential, so that you can solve for the time or the rate.

\(y = a^x\) asks “what do I get when I raise \(a\) to the power \(x\)?” \(y = \log_a x\) asks “what power of \(a\) gives \(x\)?” So \(\log_a(a^x) = x\) and \(a^{\log_a x} = x\). Their graphs are reflections of each other in the line \(y = x\): the exponential has a horizontal asymptote, the logarithm a vertical one.

Useful facts: \(a^0 = 1\) so \(\log_a 1 = 0\); \(a^1 = a\) so \(\log_a a = 1\); \(a^{-n} = \dfrac{1}{a^n}\); \(a^{\frac{1}{n}} = \sqrt[n]{a}\). The logarithm of zero or a negative number is undefined.
Same base: \(4^{x} = 8 \Rightarrow 2^{2x} = 2^3 \Rightarrow x = \tfrac{3}{2}\).
Different bases: \(3^x = 20 \Rightarrow x = \log_3 20 = \dfrac{\log_e 20}{\log_e 3} \approx 2.73\).

Combine logs with the log laws, then rewrite in index form. Example: \(\log_2 x + \log_2 (x - 2) = 3\). \(\log_2\big(x(x - 2)\big) = 3 \Rightarrow x^2 - 2x = 8 \Rightarrow (x - 4)(x + 2) = 0\). \(x = -2\) is rejected because \(\log_2(-2)\) is undefined, so \(x = 4\).

\(y = a \cdot b^{x - h} + k\) has asymptote \(y = k\). \(y = a\log_b(x - h) + k\) has asymptote \(x = h\) and domain \(x > h\). For each graph, state the asymptote with its equation, find the axis intercepts, and give one other point.
\(A = A_0 e^{kt}\) models growth when \(k > 0\) and decay when \(k < 0\). \(A_0\) is the initial amount.
Example: a population doubles every 5 years. \(2 = e^{5k} \Rightarrow k = \dfrac{\log_e 2}{5} \approx 0.139\). The time to triple is \(t = \dfrac{\log_e 3}{k} \approx 7.9\) years.
Simplify \((2x^3y^{-1})^2 \times 3xy^4\). Square each factor: \(4x^6y^{-2}\). Multiply: \(12x^7y^2\).

Fractional indices: \(8^{\frac{2}{3}} = \left(\sqrt[3]{8}\right)^2 = 4\); take the root first to keep numbers small. Negative indices: \(27^{-\frac{1}{3}} = \dfrac{1}{3}\). Write answers with positive indices unless asked otherwise.

The number \(e \approx 2.718\) is the base for which the gradient of \(y = e^x\) at any point equals its \(y\)-value. That property makes \(e^x\) the natural choice for calculus and modelling, and its inverse, \(\log_e x\), is the natural logarithm.
Any positive number can be written as a power of \(e\): \(5 = e^{\log_e 5}\). So any exponential \(y = A \cdot b^x\) can be rewritten as \(y = Ae^{kx}\) with \(k = \log_e b\).

An exponential \(y = Ae^{kx}\) passes through \((0, 3)\) and \((2, 12)\). At \(x = 0\), \(y = A = 3\). Then \(12 = 3e^{2k}\), so \(e^{2k} = 4\), \(2k = \log_e 4\) and \(k = \tfrac{1}{2}\log_e 4 = \log_e 2\).
The rule is \(y = 3e^{x\log_e 2}\), which is the same as \(y = 3 \times 2^x\): the quantity doubles each time \(x\) increases by 1.
check: \(y = Ae^{kx}\) passes through \((0, 5)\) and \((1, 5e^2)\). Find \(A\) and \(k\).

p: Writing \(\log(a + b) = \log a + \log b\). Forgetting to reject solutions that make a log undefined. Treating \((2^x)^2\) as \(2^{x^2}\). Leaving an asymptote off a sketch.

topics.title: Circular functions
points: Radians: \(\pi = 180^\circ\). On the unit circle, \(\cos\theta\) is the \(x\)-coordinate and \(\sin\theta\) the \(y\)-coordinate; \(\tan\theta = \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\).

Exact values: \(\sin\tfrac{\pi}{6} = \tfrac{1}{2}\), \(\cos\tfrac{\pi}{3} = \tfrac{1}{2}\), \(\sin\tfrac{\pi}{4} = \cos\tfrac{\pi}{4} = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\), \(\tan\tfrac{\pi}{4} = 1\), \(\sin\tfrac{\pi}{3} = \tfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\).
Signs by quadrant: All, Sin, Tan, Cos (ASTC).
\(y = a\sin(nx) + k\): amplitude \(|a|\), period \(\dfrac{2\pi}{n}\), centre line \(y = k\). \(y = \tan(nx)\) has period \(\dfrac{\pi}{n}\).
Pythagorean identity: \(\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1\).
topics.explain: Explain why \(\sin\tfrac{5\pi}{6} = \sin\tfrac{\pi}{6}\) using the unit circle.

qs.e: Reference angle π/6 in quadrant 2, where sine is positive.
Reference angle π/3 in quadrant 3, where cosine is negative.

s: Cosine is negative in quadrants 2 and 3: \(x = \pi - \tfrac{\pi}{6} = \tfrac{5\pi}{6}\) and \(x = \pi + \tfrac{\pi}{6} = \tfrac{7\pi}{6}\).

qs.q: State the amplitude, period and range of \(y = 3\sin\left(\tfrac{\pi x}{2}\right) - 1\).
s: The mean line is y = −1, so the range is from −1 − 3 to −1 + 3: [−4, 2].

p: Before this lesson you should know sine, cosine and tangent in right-angled triangles (SOH CAH TOA) and how transformations change a graph.

The big idea: circular functions describe anything that repeats: tides, sound waves, daylight hours, a Ferris wheel. The unit circle extends the triangle ratios to every angle, and radians make the functions behave well in calculus.

An angle \(\theta\) is measured anticlockwise from the positive \(x\)-axis. The point on the unit circle at that angle has coordinates \((\cos\theta, \sin\theta)\), and \(\tan\theta = \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\). One radian is the angle that cuts off an arc equal in length to the radius, so a full turn is \(2\pi\) radians. To convert, multiply degrees by \(\dfrac{\pi}{180}\).

Learn the first-quadrant values for \(\tfrac{\pi}{6}\), \(\tfrac{\pi}{4}\) and \(\tfrac{\pi}{3}\). Every other exact value comes from a reference angle and the sign for the quadrant: \(\sin(\pi - \theta) = \sin\theta\), \(\cos(\pi - \theta) = -\cos\theta\), \(\sin(\pi + \theta) = -\sin\theta\), \(\cos(2\pi - \theta) = \cos\theta\), \(\sin(-\theta) = -\sin\theta\), \(\cos(-\theta) = \cos\theta\).

Example: \(\cos\tfrac{5\pi}{6}\). The reference angle is \(\tfrac{\pi}{6}\), in the second quadrant where cosine is negative, so the value is \(-\tfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\). Complementary relationship: \(\sin\left(\tfrac{\pi}{2} - \theta\right) = \cos\theta\).

Solve \(2\sin x = 1\) for \(0 \le x \le 2\pi\). \(\sin x = \tfrac{1}{2}\); the reference angle is \(\tfrac{\pi}{6}\); sine is positive in quadrants 1 and 2, so \(x = \tfrac{\pi}{6}\) or \(\tfrac{5\pi}{6}\).

With a multiple angle, change the domain first. Solve \(\cos 2x = \tfrac{1}{2}\) for \(0 \le x \le 2\pi\): let \(\theta = 2x\) with \(0 \le \theta \le 4\pi\). \(\theta = \tfrac{\pi}{3}, \tfrac{5\pi}{3}, \tfrac{7\pi}{3}, \tfrac{11\pi}{3}\), so \(x = \tfrac{\pi}{6}, \tfrac{5\pi}{6}, \tfrac{7\pi}{6}, \tfrac{11\pi}{6}\).

For \(y = a\sin\big(n(x - h)\big) + k\): amplitude \(|a|\), period \(\dfrac{2\pi}{n}\), horizontal translation \(h\), mean position \(y = k\), range \([k - |a|, k + |a|]\). The tangent graph \(y = a\tan(nx)\) has period \(\dfrac{\pi}{n}\) and vertical asymptotes where \(\cos(nx) = 0\).
To sketch, mark the mean line, the maximum and minimum, divide one period into four equal parts and plot the key points, then label endpoints and intercepts.
The depth of water in a harbour is \(d = 3\cos\left(\tfrac{\pi}{6}t\right) + 5\) metres, \(t\) hours after midnight.

Period \(= 2\pi \div \tfrac{\pi}{6} = 12\) hours. Maximum depth 8 m at \(t = 0\) and \(t = 12\); minimum 2 m at \(t = 6\). Depth is 6.5 m when \(\cos\left(\tfrac{\pi}{6}t\right) = \tfrac{1}{2}\), so \(\tfrac{\pi}{6}t = \tfrac{\pi}{3}\) or \(\tfrac{5\pi}{3}\), giving \(t = 2\) or \(t = 10\).

notes.h: From triangles to the unit circle
p: In a right-angled triangle, \(\sin\theta = \dfrac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}}\), which only makes sense for acute angles. On the unit circle the hypotenuse is the radius, 1, so \(\sin\theta\) is simply the \(y\)-coordinate of the point. That definition works for any angle, including obtuse, reflex and negative ones.

A radian is defined by arc length: on a circle of radius \(r\), an angle of \(\theta\) radians cuts off an arc of length \(s = r\theta\). Example: \(r = 5\), \(\theta = 1.2\) gives \(s = 6\). The area of the sector is \(\tfrac{1}{2}r^2\theta\).

Sketch \(y = 2\sin(2x) + 1\) for \(0 \le x \le \pi\). Amplitude 2, period \(\dfrac{2\pi}{2} = \pi\), mean line \(y = 1\), range \([-1, 3]\). Divide one period into quarters: \((0, 1)\), \(\left(\tfrac{\pi}{4}, 3\right)\), \(\left(\tfrac{\pi}{2}, 1\right)\), \(\left(\tfrac{3\pi}{4}, -1\right)\), \((\pi, 1)\).

\(x\)-intercepts: \(\sin 2x = -\tfrac{1}{2}\). With \(0 \le 2x \le 2\pi\), \(2x = \tfrac{7\pi}{6}\) or \(\tfrac{11\pi}{6}\), so \(x = \tfrac{7\pi}{12}\) or \(\tfrac{11\pi}{12}\). Label the endpoints, the maximum, the minimum and the intercepts.

\(\tan\theta = \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\). It is the gradient of the line from the origin to the point on the unit circle. It is undefined wherever \(\cos\theta = 0\), giving vertical asymptotes at \(\theta = \tfrac{\pi}{2} + k\pi\). Exact values: \(\tan\tfrac{\pi}{6} = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\), \(\tan\tfrac{\pi}{4} = 1\), \(\tan\tfrac{\pi}{3} = \sqrt{3}\).
Solve \(\tan x = -1\) for \(0 \le x \le 2\pi\): the reference angle is \(\tfrac{\pi}{4}\), and tangent is negative in quadrants 2 and 4, so \(x = \tfrac{3\pi}{4}\) or \(\tfrac{7\pi}{4}\).
check: What is the exact value of \(\tan\tfrac{5\pi}{4}\)?
1. The reference angle is \(\tfrac{\pi}{4}\), and tangent is positive in the third quadrant.

p: Calculator in degree mode. Finding only one solution in the domain. Dividing both sides by \(\sin x\) and losing solutions where \(\sin x = 0\). Giving the period of tangent as \(2\pi\).

topics.title: Rates of change
points: Average rate of change between two points is the gradient of the chord (secant) joining them.
Instantaneous rate of change is the gradient of the tangent at a point.
The instantaneous rate is found as the limit of average rates over smaller and smaller intervals.
Rates have units: the units of the output per unit of the input.
On a distance–time graph the gradient is speed; on a displacement–time graph it is velocity.
topics.explain: A car travels 120 km in 2 hours. Explain why its average speed is 60 km/h even though the speedometer may never have shown exactly 60.

p: Before this lesson you should know how to find the gradient of a straight line and be comfortable with function notation.

The big idea: calculus begins with one question: how fast is something changing at a particular moment? For a straight line the answer is its gradient. For a curve the gradient keeps changing, so we approach it through average rates over shorter and shorter intervals. This lesson builds the idea that the next lesson turns into a rule.
The average rate of change of \(f\) from \(x = a\) to \(x = b\) is \(\dfrac{f(b) - f(a)}{b - a}\). It is the gradient of the straight line (chord) joining the two points on the graph.

Example: a population is \(P(t) = 200 + 10t^2\) after \(t\) years. From \(t = 1\) to \(t = 3\): \(\dfrac{P(3) - P(1)}{3 - 1} = \dfrac{290 - 210}{2} = 40\) people per year. The population did not grow by exactly 40 each year; 40 is the steady rate that would give the same overall change.
check: Find the average rate of change of \(f(x) = x^3\) from \(x = 1\) to \(x = 2\).

p: The instantaneous rate at a point is the gradient of the tangent there. From a graph, draw a tangent by eye, pick two points on it and find its gradient. This gives an estimate.

For a better answer, take average rates over shrinking intervals. For \(P(t) = 200 + 10t^2\) at \(t = 1\): from 1 to 2, the rate is 30; from 1 to 1.1, it is 21; from 1 to 1.01, it is 20.1; from 1 to 1.001, it is 20.01. The values approach 20, so the instantaneous rate at \(t = 1\) is 20 people per year.
check: For \(f(x) = x^2\), the average rates from \(x = 3\) to \(3.1\), \(3.01\) and \(3.001\) are 6.1, 6.01 and 6.001. What is the instantaneous rate at \(x = 3\)?

p: The process above is a limit. Writing \(h\) for the width of the interval, the average rate from \(x\) to \(x + h\) is \(\dfrac{f(x + h) - f(x)}{h}\), and the instantaneous rate is the value this approaches as \(h \to 0\).

We cannot simply put \(h = 0\), because that gives \(\dfrac{0}{0}\). Instead simplify first. For \(f(x) = x^2\): \(\dfrac{(x + h)^2 - x^2}{h} = \dfrac{2xh + h^2}{h} = 2x + h\), which approaches \(2x\) as \(h \to 0\). At \(x = 3\) this gives 6, matching the numerical estimate. This is differentiation from first principles, covered in full in the next lesson.

The units of a rate are output units per input unit: litres per minute, dollars per item, metres per second. On a displacement–time graph the gradient is velocity; on a velocity–time graph it is acceleration.

Reading graphs: a steeper section means a faster rate; a horizontal section means zero rate (the quantity is momentarily not changing); a negative gradient means the quantity is decreasing. A curve that gets steeper is increasing at an increasing rate.
Subtracting in different orders on the top and bottom of the rate formula. Leaving out units. Confusing average and instantaneous rates. Substituting \(h = 0\) before simplifying.

qs.q: The average rate of change of \(f(x) = x^2\) from \(x = 1\) to \(x = 4\) is…
The instantaneous rate of change at a point is the gradient of the…
Simplify \(\dfrac{(x + h)^2 - x^2}{h}\) and state its limit as \(h \to 0\).
On a displacement–time graph, a horizontal section means…
Water volume \(V\) (litres) is measured against time \(t\) (minutes). What are the units of the rate of change?
Find the average rate of change of \(f(x) = 2x^2 + 1\) from \(x = 1\) to \(x = 3\).
A car travels 150 km in 2.5 hours. Its average speed is…
Simplify \(\dfrac{(x + h)^3 - x^3}{h}\) and find its limit as \(h \to 0\).
On a distance–time graph, a steeper section means the object is…
The cost of producing \(n\) items is \(C(n) = 100 + 2n - 0.01n^2\) dollars. Find the average rate of change of cost from \(n = 10\) to \(n = 20\).

topics.title: Differentiation
points: The derivative is the gradient of the tangent. First principles: \[f'(x) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(x + h) - f(x)}{h}\]
Power rule: \(\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(x^n\right) = nx^{n-1}\). The derivative of a constant is \(0\).
Tangent at \(x = a\): \(y - f(a) = f'(a)(x - a)\).
Stationary points where \(f'(x) = 0\): local maximum, local minimum or stationary point of inflection (check the sign of \(f'(x)\) either side).
Average rate of change \(= \dfrac{f(b) - f(a)}{b - a}\). Instantaneous rate of change \(= f'(x)\).
topics.explain: Explain how you can tell a maximum from a minimum using a sign diagram of \(f'(x)\).

qs.q: Find the stationary points of \(y = x^3 - 3x\).
Find the equation of the tangent to \(y = x^2\) at \(x = 1\).
Find the average rate of change of \(f(x) = x^2\) from \(x = 1\) to \(x = 3\).
Find the equation of the tangent to \(y = x^2 - 3x\) at \(x = 4\).
Find and classify the stationary points of \(y = x^3 - 12x\).
s: The gradient is positive, then negative, then positive, so \((-2, 16)\) is a local maximum and \((2, -16)\) a local minimum.

qs.q: If \(f'(x) > 0\) for all \(x\) in an interval, then on that interval \(f\) is…

p: Before this lesson you should have worked through the rates of change lesson and be confident with gradients and index laws.

The big idea: the derivative gives the rate of change of a function at every point. With one rule for powers of \(x\), you can find gradients, tangents, maximums and minimums, and answer real questions about speed, growth and optimal design.

The average rate of change between two points is the gradient of the chord joining them. As the second point moves closer to the first, the chord approaches the tangent, and its gradient approaches the instantaneous rate of change. That limit is the derivative. \(f'(x)\) and \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\) both mean the gradient function.
Differentiate \(f(x) = x^2 + 3x\) from first principles.

\(f'(x) = \lim_{h \to 0} \dfrac{(x + h)^2 + 3(x + h) - x^2 - 3x}{h} = \lim_{h \to 0} \dfrac{2xh + h^2 + 3h}{h} = \lim_{h \to 0}(2x + h + 3) = 2x + 3\). Keep writing the limit until \(h\) has been set to zero.

Rewrite before differentiating: \(\dfrac{1}{x^2} = x^{-2}\), \(\sqrt{x} = x^{\frac{1}{2}}\), and expand brackets. Example: \(y = \dfrac{4}{x} + 3\sqrt{x}\) becomes \(y = 4x^{-1} + 3x^{\frac{1}{2}}\), so \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = -4x^{-2} + \tfrac{3}{2}x^{-\frac{1}{2}}\).
Example: \(f(x) = x^3 - 3x^2 - 9x + 5\). \(f'(x) = 3x^2 - 6x - 9 = 3(x - 3)(x + 1)\), so stationary points are at \(x = -1\) and \(x = 3\).

Nature, using a sign diagram of \(f'\): for \(x < -1\) the gradient is positive, between \(-1\) and \(3\) it is negative, and for \(x > 3\) positive. So \((-1, 10)\) is a local maximum and \((3, -22)\) is a local minimum. If the gradient has the same sign on both sides, the point is a stationary point of inflection.
check: What is the gradient of the tangent to \(y = x^3\) at \(x = 2\)?

p: To maximise or minimise: write the quantity as a function of one variable (use the constraint to eliminate the other), differentiate, solve \(f'(x) = 0\), justify the nature, check endpoints of the domain, and answer in words with units.
Example: a rectangle with perimeter 20 m. \(A = x(10 - x) = 10x - x^2\). \(A' = 10 - 2x = 0\) at \(x = 5\); the parabola is inverted, so this is a maximum of 25 m².
For motion in a straight line, velocity is \(v = \dfrac{dx}{dt}\) and acceleration is \(a = \dfrac{dv}{dt}\). The particle is at rest when \(v = 0\).

\(f'(x)\) and \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\) both mean the derivative. Its units are the units of \(y\) per unit of \(x\). If \(V\) litres of water remain in a tank after \(t\) minutes, \(\dfrac{dV}{dt}\) is in litres per minute, and a negative value means the volume is decreasing.
Example: \(V = 100 - 4t^2\). \(\dfrac{dV}{dt} = -8t\). At \(t = 3\), the rate is \(-24\) L/min: water is draining at 24 litres per minute at that instant.
check: The height of a ball is \(h = 20t - 5t^2\) metres. What is its vertical velocity at \(t = 1\)?

p: Given \(f\), you can sketch \(f'\) without a rule. Wherever \(f\) has a stationary point, \(f'\) crosses or touches the \(x\)-axis. Where \(f\) increases, \(f'\) is above the axis; where it decreases, \(f'\) is below.

Example: \(f(x) = x^3 - 3x\) has stationary points at \(x = \pm 1\). \(f'(x) = 3x^2 - 3\) is a parabola that is zero at \(x = \pm 1\), positive outside them and negative between. In general the derivative of a degree \(n\) polynomial has degree \(n - 1\).

notes.h: Worked example: a full curve sketch
p: Sketch \(f(x) = x^3 - 6x^2 + 9x\). Factorise: \(f(x) = x(x - 3)^2\), so it crosses at \(x = 0\) and touches at \(x = 3\).

\(f'(x) = 3x^2 - 12x + 9 = 3(x - 1)(x - 3)\). Stationary points at \(x = 1\) and \(x = 3\). \(f(1) = 4\) and \(f(3) = 0\). The sign of \(f'\) is positive, then negative, then positive, so \((1, 4)\) is a local maximum and \((3, 0)\) a local minimum. A positive cubic rises from bottom left to top right, which agrees.
check: Find the stationary point of \(y = x^2 - 6x + 1\) and state its nature.
\(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 2x - 6 = 0\) at \(x = 3\); \(y = -8\). It is a local minimum (an upright parabola).

p: Differentiating a constant to itself instead of 0. Dropping the limit notation in first principles. Stating a maximum without showing the sign of the gradient either side. Forgetting to find the \(y\)-coordinate.

topics.title: Anti-differentiation
points: \(\displaystyle\int x^n \, dx = \frac{x^{n+1}}{n + 1} + c\), for \(n \neq -1\).
Always add the constant \(c\); use a given point to find it.
If \(f'(x)\) is given, \(f(x)\) is its antiderivative.
Anti-differentiate term by term.

s: Raise each power by one and divide by the new power: \(\tfrac{6x^3}{3} - \tfrac{4x^2}{2} + x\).
Simplify and add the constant: \(2x^3 - 2x^2 + x + c\).

qs.q: A particle has velocity \(v = 4t + 1\) m/s and starts at \(x = 2\) m. Find its position at \(t = 3\).

s: Raise the power to \(\tfrac{3}{2}\) and divide by \(\tfrac{3}{2}\): \(\tfrac{2}{3}x^{\frac{3}{2}} + c\).

qs.q: \(f'(x) = 2x - 4\). The graph of \(f\) has a stationary point at…

p: Before this lesson you should be confident with differentiation and with rewriting expressions as powers of \(x\).

The big idea: anti-differentiation works backwards from a rate of change to the original quantity. If you know how fast something is changing and where it started, you can reconstruct it. In Units 3 and 4 this becomes integration and the area under a curve.

Anti-differentiation asks: which function has this derivative? Because the derivative of any constant is zero, there is a whole family of answers that differ by a constant, so the general antiderivative includes \(+ c\). Each value of \(c\) gives a vertical translation of the same curve.
Rewrite each term as a power of \(x\), raise the power by one, and divide by the new power. Check by differentiating your answer.
Example: \(\displaystyle\int \left(6x^2 - \frac{4}{x^3} + \sqrt{x}\right)dx = \int \left(6x^2 - 4x^{-3} + x^{\frac{1}{2}}\right)dx = 2x^3 + 2x^{-2} + \tfrac{2}{3}x^{\frac{3}{2}} + c\).
A condition, such as a point on the curve, fixes \(c\). Example: \(f'(x) = 3x^2 - 4\) and \(f(1) = 2\). \(f(x) = x^3 - 4x + c\); \(1 - 4 + c = 2\) gives \(c = 5\), so \(f(x) = x^3 - 4x + 5\).

Velocity is the derivative of position, so position is an antiderivative of velocity. Example: \(v = 6t - 2\) and the particle starts at \(x = 3\). \(x = 3t^2 - 2t + c\); at \(t = 0\), \(x = 3\), so \(x = 3t^2 - 2t + 3\).

Given the graph of \(f'\), sketch \(f\): where \(f'\) is positive, \(f\) increases; where \(f'\) is zero, \(f\) has a stationary point; where \(f'\) changes from positive to negative, \(f\) has a local maximum. Without a given point, any vertical translation is acceptable.
Expand products: \(\displaystyle\int (x + 1)^2\,dx = \int (x^2 + 2x + 1)\,dx = \frac{x^3}{3} + x^2 + x + c\).
Split fractions over a single term: \(\displaystyle\int \frac{x^2 + 3}{x^2}\,dx = \int \left(1 + 3x^{-2}\right)dx = x - 3x^{-1} + c\).
Convert roots: \(\displaystyle\int \sqrt{x}(x - 1)\,dx = \int \left(x^{\frac{3}{2}} - x^{\frac{1}{2}}\right)dx = \tfrac{2}{5}x^{\frac{5}{2}} - \tfrac{2}{3}x^{\frac{3}{2}} + c\).

notes.h: A first look at area under a curve
p: The area under a curve can be estimated with rectangles. For \(y = x^2\) on \([0, 2]\) with four strips of width 0.5, using the right endpoint of each strip as the height: \(0.5(0.25 + 1 + 2.25 + 4) = 3.75\).

The exact area turns out to be \(\tfrac{8}{3} \approx 2.67\). Right endpoints overestimate for an increasing function; left endpoints underestimate. Narrower strips give better estimates, and in Units 3 and 4 the limit of this process is the definite integral, which is calculated with antiderivatives.
check: For an increasing function, do left-endpoint rectangles overestimate or underestimate the area?
Underestimate: each rectangle uses the lowest height on its strip.

p: Leaving out \(+ c\). Dividing by the old power. Integrating a product or quotient term by term without expanding first. Trying to use the rule for \(x^{-1}\); that case gives a logarithm, covered in Units 3 and 4.

topics.title: Probability and counting
points: Addition rule: \(\Pr(A \cup B) = \Pr(A) + \Pr(B) - \Pr(A \cap B)\).
Conditional probability: \(\Pr(A \mid B) = \dfrac{\Pr(A \cap B)}{\Pr(B)}\). Independent if \(\Pr(A \cap B) = \Pr(A)\Pr(B)\).
Use Venn diagrams, Karnaugh maps, tree diagrams and two-way tables.
Arrangements: \(n!\). Permutations: \({}^nP_r = \dfrac{n!}{(n - r)!}\). Combinations: \(\displaystyle\binom{n}{r} = \frac{n!}{r!\,(n - r)!}\).
topics.explain: Explain the difference between mutually exclusive and independent events.

qs.q: \(\Pr(A) = 0.5\), \(\Pr(B) = 0.4\), and \(A\), \(B\) are independent. Find \(\Pr(A \cap B)\) and \(\Pr(A \cup B)\).
How many ways can 2 people be chosen from 5?
How many ways can the letters of MATH be arranged?
\(\Pr(A) = 0.5\), \(\Pr(B) = 0.4\) and \(\Pr(A \cup B) = 0.7\). Find \(\Pr(A \cap B)\) and decide whether \(A\) and \(B\) are independent.
s: These are equal, so A and B are independent.

qs.q: Two fair dice are rolled. Find the probability that the sum is 7.
How many different arrangements are there of the letters of MATHS?
Two students are chosen at random from 4 boys and 3 girls. Find the probability that both are girls.

p: Before this lesson you should be comfortable with fractions, decimals and percentages.

The big idea: probability measures how likely an event is on a scale from 0 to 1. A few rules, and a few ways of organising information (tables, diagrams and counting), let you calculate the probability of complicated events from simple ones. This is the foundation for the statistics in Units 3 and 4.

The sample space is the set of all outcomes; an event is a subset of it. \(A \cap B\) is “\(A\) and \(B\)”; \(A \cup B\) is “\(A\) or \(B\) or both”; \(A'\) is “not \(A\)”. Mutually exclusive events cannot happen together, so \(\Pr(A \cap B) = 0\). Independent events do not affect each other, so \(\Pr(A \cap B) = \Pr(A)\Pr(B)\). These are different ideas: mutually exclusive events with non-zero probabilities are never independent.

A probability table with \(A\) and \(A'\) as columns and \(B\) and \(B'\) as rows. Rows and columns add to the marginal totals, and the grand total is 1. Fill in what is given and complete the rest by adding or subtracting.

\(\Pr(A \mid B)\) is the probability of \(A\) given that \(B\) has happened: the sample space shrinks to \(B\). From the example above, \(\Pr(A \mid B) = \dfrac{0.1}{0.4} = 0.25\). Since this is not equal to \(\Pr(A) = 0.5\), the events are not independent.
Tree diagrams suit multi-stage experiments. Multiply along branches for “and”; add between branches for “or”. Second-stage branches carry conditional probabilities.
A bag has 3 red and 2 blue marbles. Two are drawn without replacement. Find the probability they are different colours.

\(\Pr(RB) = \tfrac{3}{5} \times \tfrac{2}{4} = \tfrac{3}{10}\) and \(\Pr(BR) = \tfrac{2}{5} \times \tfrac{3}{4} = \tfrac{3}{10}\). Total \(= \tfrac{3}{5}\). Given that the second is red, the probability the first was blue is \(\dfrac{\Pr(BR)}{\Pr(\text{second red})} = \dfrac{3/10}{3/10 + 3/10} = \tfrac{1}{2}\).

Multiplication principle: if one choice can be made in \(m\) ways and the next in \(n\) ways, there are \(mn\) ways together. Use arrangements when order matters and selections (combinations) when it does not.

Example: choose a committee of 3 from 8 people: \({}^8C_3 = \dfrac{8!}{3!\,5!} = 56\). Choose a president, secretary and treasurer from 8: \(8 \times 7 \times 6 = 336\). Probability a random committee of 3 includes two particular people: choose 1 more from the other 6, so \(\dfrac{6}{56} = \tfrac{3}{28}\).

When outcomes are not equally likely, estimate probability from experiments or data: relative frequency \(= \dfrac{\text{number of times the event occurs}}{\text{number of trials}}\). Example: a drawing pin lands point up 124 times in 200 tosses, so \(\Pr(\text{up}) \approx 0.62\).

The more trials, the closer the relative frequency tends to be to the true probability. Simulation, using random numbers on a calculator or computer, applies the same idea when real trials would be slow or expensive.

When all selections are equally likely, \(\Pr = \dfrac{\text{number of favourable selections}}{\text{total number of selections}}\). Example: 3 balls are chosen from a bag of 10, of which 4 are red. \(\Pr(\text{all red}) = \dfrac{{}^4C_3}{{}^{10}C_3} = \dfrac{4}{120} = \dfrac{1}{30}\).
Useful facts: \({}^nC_r = {}^nC_{n-r}\), and the values of \({}^nC_r\) form Pascal’s triangle, where each entry is the sum of the two above it.

\(\Pr(A) = 0.4\), \(\Pr(B) = 0.5\), \(\Pr(A \cap B) = 0.2\). Since \(0.4 \times 0.5 = 0.2\), the events are independent. Also \(\Pr(A \cup B) = 0.4 + 0.5 - 0.2 = 0.7\), and \(\Pr(A \mid B) = \dfrac{0.2}{0.5} = 0.4 = \Pr(A)\), which confirms it: knowing \(B\) occurred does not change the probability of \(A\).

Adding probabilities of events that overlap without subtracting the intersection. Confusing \(\Pr(A \mid B)\) with \(\Pr(B \mid A)\). Treating draws without replacement as independent. Using permutations when order does not matter.
